items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Benny Waters, the tenor sax man that I had worked with in Charlie Johnson Small's Paradise orchestra... The replacement for Dickie Wells was Benny Waters whom I had worked with in Charlie Johnson's orchestra.

ctx.x: Dickie Wells was playing with Charlie Johnson who left Small's Paradise in 1931. Charlie asked Frank Newton and myself to join his band. I accepted because Charlie was better known than Neal and the salary would be better also. The members of Charlie's band were Ben Witted,
Harvey Boone, alto sax, Benny Waters, tenor, Bobby Johnson, guitar, Dell Thomas, bass, Leonard 'Ham' Davis, Frank and myself on trumpets, Dickie on trombone and George Stafford, drums.

The band went on tour and Sidney de Paris was added which made four trumpets and gave the brass section an even bigger sound and more punch than it had before. For my money, Charlie Johnson had a band that was second to Fletcher Henderson and he used to give Fletcher some tough battles before I joined the band.

items.title: 68002_Benny Waters oral history interview
items.q: Then Bill and, Bill asked me, would I want to join the band.

ctx.x: Yeah. So then Dicky Wells just got tired. We didn't even have Zutty Singleton on the job, we had Zutty there with him. And Zutty got tired, you can read that thing in "Down Beat" about that, too, Zutty did. He got tired, he said all musicians in Europe were starving, which is not true, see. That's what he said, see. But it was a lot of musicians out of work (laughs), that, you know, is true. Negro musicians, I mean, is true. So I had a chance to join him on account of Dicky Wells just got tired and left. It was…
'Cause you knew Coleman would end up in Paris sooner or later -

items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: I rang Mickey Baker, guitarist, Kenny Clark, drummer, Art Simmons, piano, Benny Water, sax-tenor... We did the show

ctx.x: I went back to play at the Trois Mailletz. I had been angry for some time with Madame Calvé, but decided to forget the difference. Past was past, and it's nice sometimes to play in a club. Another club where I started to play was the Caveau de la Huchette, also situated in the Latin Quarter, which had been bought by Danny Doris, the vibraphonist with whom I had worked quite a few times. The atmosphere of the Huchette was more easier going than at the Trois Mailletz, where people came more to listen to music. In…

A famous well known French composer and singer, Guy Béart, contacted me. He had a T.V. programme called "Bienvenue" which means "Welcome" to Guy Béart. He wss having that programme about twice a month, andhe was inviting all kinds of personalities for his show. He told me that he wanted to make a show called "Bienvenue to American artists", and asked me if I was willing to contact the American musicians available in Paris. I rang Mickey Baker, guitarist, Kenny Clark, drummer, Art Simmons, piano, Benny Water,…

We were all very excited to be with Duke. He came on the T.V. set at 5 p.m., dressed in a light blue costume(it was in July). Guy Béart introduced him to the audience, because Guy Béart always had his emission semi-public with personalities, artists, guests, press, and a lot of beautiful girls, who were engaged especially to add more class to the show.
